about: Namnetis (Nantes), the bishop's city on the Loire at the edge of the Breton march, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/namnetis.md and the spine (cast.alcuin; threads book_road, dorestad_falls, riddle_road). A draft for the user to overwrite. Read the note first.
note: What is known of Nantes in these years comes mostly from one hostile canon writing about 1050 (the Chronicle of Nantes) and from a few lines of the royal annals. No merchant, moneyer, shipwright, pilot or toll man of the city is named anywhere, and nobody knows who was count in 793. So the bishops, the counts and Alan are real and dated, and the toll man, the pilot, the ale-wife and the English monk are ours, built from the kinds of people the charter of 857 lists (toll-gatherers, ale-house keepers, carters, market sellers) and each says so in its source. The miracles are told as stories people tell. Alan and the Bretons are given the people 'romance' because the roles table has no Breton people (see the report's needs).
woven: Woven with Quentovic, Rotomagus, Parisius, Herio and Burdigala on 6 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways; made real here: namnetis.rainald (Count Rainald of Herbauge, whom the Herio file named) and namnetis.cooper (whom the Rotomagus cooper named); Alan's tie to the Northmen's count at Rouen now points at rotomagus.longsword; his tie to King Athelstan, his godfather, was taken out by the period editor on 7 Oct 2026, because no places file has that king as a person (the fact stands in Alan's source and in his lines: put the tie back if the Lundenwic file gains him); beats placed across the region and the port's cards (encounters/neustria_west_793.json) put on their sites. Nothing was taken out.

ports.summary: Namnetis is an old Roman bishop's city of the Franks on the north bank of the Loire, where the Erdre runs in: a wall of sixteen hectares too big for the people inside it, a cathedral with a tin roof, and a port under the wall that takes the king's toll on everything that comes by ship or any other way. West of it the Bretons begin, and the count who holds the city holds the march against them. A merchant comes for bay salt in autumn and Loire wine after the vintage, for river fish, for the Saint John's gathering when the whole country is in the streets, and because this is the mouth of the road to Tours, where the best books in Gaul are being written.
ports.seasons: The river is high and brown with snow water in spring and runs thin over its sandbanks by Lammas; ice comes down it in a hard winter. Saints Donatian and Rogatian are kept on 24 May; on Saint John's day, 24 June, pilgrims come from far cities and the night before is a vigil at his church. Salt comes up from the bay from the Assumption to Saint Luke's day, wine comes down after the vintage, the cathedral keeps its dedication on the last day of September, and by Martinmas the sea trade is over.

history.text: After this year the city is walled: 1,665 metres round, about eight metres high and four thick, with round towers at the corners, along the Erdre and the Loire. It encloses 16 hectares (18 by another count).
history.source: fr.wikipedia Enceinte gallo-romaine de Nantes; fr.wikipedia Histoire de Nantes (dossier 1-2)

history.text: About now Bishop Felix dedicates his basilica of Saints Peter and Paul on 30 September: three naves, a tin roof, marble columns. He also cuts a channel to bring the river to the city's port. (The dedication fell between 567 and 573.)
history.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 1 and Merlet's notes (ed. Merlet 1896); fr.wikipedia Felix de Nantes; fr.wikipedia Cathedrale Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul de Nantes

history.text: About now a ship lies at Nantes that has brought Irish wares; the bishop and the count put the exiled abbot Columban aboard her to be sent home to Ireland.
history.source: Jonas, Life of St Columban c. 47, tr. D. C. Munro (Fordham sourcebook)

history.text: About now Hermeland founds his monastery on the island of Indre, three leagues below the city, in water rich in fish.
history.source: fr.wikipedia Hermeland d'Indre; Chronicon Namnetense c. 6 (dossier 2)

history.text: About now Odilard becomes bishop; he is bishop still when the game begins and until about 800.
history.source: fr.wikipedia Liste des eveques de Nantes (dossier 3)

history.text: This year Count Wido, who presided in the march of Brittany, went through the whole of that land with his fellow counts and brought King Charles the weapons of the chiefs who had yielded, each marked with its owner's name.
About now Alcuin, abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours, writes for Count Wido a short book on the virtues and the vices, for a man busy with war.
history.source: en.wikipedia Alcuin (dossier 3); the date within 796-804 is from memory (?)

history.text: An army is sent against the Bretons to punish their breach of faith.
From the reign of the emperor Louis pennies are struck here reading NAMNETVM, of 1.78 grams. (None is known for King Charles.)
history.source: M. Prou, Les monnaies carolingiennes (1896), pp. 92-93 (dossier 2, 8)

history.text: Count Wido is dead by now; Lambert holds the county until 831, and Ricuin after him.
history.source: fr.wikipedia Guy de Nantes; fr.wikipedia Liste des comtes de Nantes

history.text: Gunhard becomes bishop.
history.source: fr.wikipedia Liste des eveques de Nantes; fr.wikipedia Gohard de Nantes

history.text: On 25 June Count Ricuin dies in the battle at Fontenoy. King Charles gives Nantes to Renaud of Herbauges and not to Lambert, who goes over to the Bretons.
history.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 4; fr.wikipedia Lambert II de Nantes

history.text: On 24 May Lambert and the Bretons kill Count Renaud at Blain. On Saint John's day, 24 June, Northmen come up the river on a west wind, climb the wall with ladders, break in by an entrance long since blocked, kill Bishop Gunhard and the crowd in the cathedral, and leave at dusk with captives. On 29 June they burn Indre. On 30 September the cathedral is cleansed and Mass is said again.
history.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 4-7; Annales Bertiniani 843; chronicle_793.json 843-06-24-nantes-sacked. That Lambert guided the fleet is the chronicle's story of c. 1050 and may be legend (dossier 8)

history.text: Lambert and Nominoe of the Bretons take Nantes and throw down its walls.
history.source: fr.wikipedia Lambert II de Nantes; Merlet 1896 (dossier 5)

history.text: King Charles grants Erispoe of the Bretons Rennes, Nantes and Retz. The city is Breton from now on.
In July Danes from the Seine plunder Nantes; they hold the islands of the Loire until 856.

Erispoe gives the bishop back half the toll of all goods that come to the port of the city, by ship or any other way: markets, cart-toll, wheel-toll, all ale-houses and workshops, gathered by the bishop's own men. He makes the gift by a gold-trimmed key of Saint Peter's relics.
The king writes that Nantes, once most flourishing, has been a desert for ten years.
Northmen beaten on the Loire ask to stay on an island in the river until February and to hold a market there.
Northmen again; Bishop Landran flees to Angers until about 889.
Bishop Landran dies on 5 February. Fulcher, bishop until about 910, rebuilds and lengthens the cathedral and walls a refuge round it.
Northmen take Nantes. The people hold the castle one day and flee by night; the cathedral burns; Bishop Adalard flees.
Robert besieges the Northmen of the Loire five months, then yields them Nantes and Brittany. A second siege of five weeks fails in 927.

Alan, called Twisted-beard, come back from the English king's court, beats the Northmen in Saint Aignan's meadow and enters a city deserted for many years, cutting his way to the cathedral door through brambles with his sword.
Alan dies and is buried, in the end, in Notre-Dame, which he rebuilt. Fulk the Good of Anjou is guardian of his son until 960.
Northmen seize Bishop Walter; after eight days the townsmen drive them off, and ransom is paid at Guerande.
history.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 38; Miracula ecclesiae Namnetensis c. 1

history.text: Count Hoel is murdered; his brother Guerech, count and bishop both, fights Conan of Rennes at Conquereuil and rebuilds the east end of the cathedral before 988.
Conan of Rennes takes Nantes and builds a castle, the Bouffay, in the western corner by the Loire. On 27 June 992 he dies at Conquereuil against Fulk Nerra of Anjou.
history.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 44; fr.wikipedia Chateau du Bouffay

history.text: About now Count Budic razes the bishop's palace while Bishop Walter is away at Jerusalem; war, then peace.
Bishop Budic, who had the see from his father, is deposed for simony at the council of Reims.
Hoel, count of Nantes, becomes duke of Brittany.

eras.text: King Charles's years and Count Wido's. A quiet, half-empty walled city with a working port under it: the king's toll, bay salt and Loire wine, pilgrims at midsummer, old Bishop Odilard and then his successors in Felix's church. No mint yet. From 796 the monks of Tours send down for calfskins and send books out. In 799 the count rides through Brittany and comes back with a cart of named weapons.

The emperor Louis's years. Pennies are struck in the city with its name on them. The counts change (Lambert, Ricuin, Renaud) and quarrel; from 835 Gunhard is bishop. The monks of Herio leave their island for good in 836 and the salt men of the bay bring their business and their talk to Nantes. Every summer somebody on the quay has seen sails.

The year of Saint John's day and after. The cathedral is stripped and for three months unclean; Indre is black posts on its island; half the families have somebody dead or sold. Bishop Actard holds on. Captives come home one at a time, bought back dear, and the market is small and frightened.

A Breton city with its walls thrown down. Danes sit on the river islands from 853 to 856 and come back whenever they like; for ten years about 860 the place is called a desert. The toll belongs half to the bishop from 857. About 900 Bishop Fulcher rebuilds the cathedral and walls a refuge round it, and for a few years ships lie under it again.

The Northmen's town. Ragenold and then Incon hold the river; the cathedral is roofless and brambles grow in the nave; a few poor Bretons till the soil. There is no toll but what the chief's men ask and no law but his, yet salt and loot are sold on the strand, and a merchant with nerve and a Norse tongue aboard can trade.

Alan's city and his heirs'. A great earthwork and a tower by the cathedral, Notre-Dame rebuilt, the canons home, the toll shared in three. After 952 Fulk of Anjou takes sacks of its pennies; in 960 the townsmen themselves drive Northmen off. The port fills again, slowly, with salt, wine and fish.

A count's town between Rennes and Anjou. The Bouffay castle stands at the river corner, the bishops are counts' sons and quarrel with the counts, and the salt of Guerande and the wine of the Loire go out in more hulls each year. A knight's household drinks where the carters used to.

sites.name: The port under the wall
sites.see: A strand of timber staging and beached hulls under the long grey river wall, from the Erdre mouth down to Bishop Felix's channel. In front, flat barges with towing masts and round salt boats from the bay, porters in the mud to their knees; behind, the wall with its round corner tower and one tin roof shining over it. Across the brown water, low islands of willow and sand and the south bank at Reze. A smell of wet salt sacks, river mud and wine lees.
sites.source: The city's port and its toll: Chronicon Namnetense c. 14. The Roman port from Richebourg to Port-Maillard and Felix's channel: fr.wikipedia Port de Nantes, Felix de Nantes. The islands: en.wikipedia Nantes. The staging is ours

sites.name: The toll bench
sites.see: A plank bench and a locked chest under a lean-to against the wall, by the gate up from the strand. A man with a tally stick and a boy with a balance sit facing the boats; carts wait in a line behind, wheels counted as they pass. Everything that comes by ship or any other way stops here first.
sites.source: The toll on all goods coming to the port by ship or any other way, with cart-toll and wheel-toll, gathered by named kinds of men: Chronicon Namnetense c. 14 (857), carried back to 793 as the king's and the count's. From about 940 it is split in three: c. 31

sites.name: The market inside the gate
sites.see: A wide paved street of the old Roman town, grass between the stones, with trestles down both sides: grey salt in open sacks, casks on their bilges, strings of dried lamprey, baskets of shad on wet leaves, Breton grain, pots. Roofless Roman walls behind serve as pens and stores. Carters shout for room, a clerk's bell rings from the cathedral, and somebody is always frying fish.
sites.source: Markets that paid toll: Chronicon Namnetense c. 14. Salt, wine and river fish: dossier 4. The street and the stalls are ours; the shad and lamprey are the Loire's own fish, not in any text of these years (?)

sites.name: Saints Peter and Paul
sites.see: Bishop Felix's church by the east wall: three naves under a roof of tin, marble columns, walls of small coloured stones, gold crowns hanging over the altars and a great crucifix held from the beam by a silver chain. On one column sits a red stone from Alexandria that is said to give light at night. Lamp smoke, old incense, the cold of marble; clerks chanting behind a screen.
sites.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 1 (the altars, crowns, crucifix and carbuncle); fr.wikipedia Cathedrale Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul de Nantes (three naves, the tin roof). Wrecked 843, rebuilt about 900, burned 919, roofless 937, east end rebuilt 981-988: the eras say which church the player sees

sites.name: Saint John the Baptist's
sites.see: A small old church near the cathedral with a basin for baptism sunk in its floor and a porch black with candle smoke. On most days two clerks and a sweeping woman. On the eve of the saint it cannot be seen for people: pilgrims asleep against the walls, sellers of wax and bread, a vigil that lasts till light.
sites.source: The pilgrims' goal on Saint John's day, with a night vigil kept by its clerks: Miracula ecclesiae Namnetensis c. 4; Chronicon Namnetense c. 6 (pilgrims from far cities). It is the church called Saint-Jean-du-Baptistere, built in the 4th or 5th century on the north side of the cathedral and found in the digs of 1910-1913 (fr.wikipedia Cathedrale Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul de Nantes): a baptistery, so the basin follows

sites.name: The ale-house by the carters' gate
sites.see: A low room built into the back of the wall beside the gate the carts use, its door open on the street. Casks on a rack, benches polished by carters, a hearth in the middle with the smoke going out through the thatch, a tally of chalk strokes on a beam. Beyond the back door, a shed stacked with salt sacks. Sour ale, woodsmoke, wet wool, and everybody's business.
sites.source: All the ale-houses of the city paid toll in 857: Chronicon Namnetense c. 14. A gate called Porta Cararia, next to the bishop's postern, is named about 940: c. 31. The house and its keeper are ours. From 836 the keeper of the salt shed behind it holds Aldhelm's riddle of the wine cask (riddles_793.json, the set salt_to_pepper)

sites.name: The count's house
sites.see: A big Roman house inside the wall, patched with timber, where the count sits when he is in the city: a hall with a painted wall gone pale, spears stacked by the door, hounds, a clerk at a table of wax tablets. Men of the march come and go in riding dress. It is no fortress; the city wall is all the castle there is.
sites.source: ours: where the count lived is not known, and no castle stood before about 900 (dossier 8). The count as guard of the march: Annales regni Francorum 799

sites.name: The castle by the cathedral
sites.see: A wall thrown round the cathedral and its houses: first Bishop Fulcher's refuge of about 900, then, on the same line, Alan's great bank of earth with a ditch and a timber tower where he lives. From the tower the whole river shows, both ways. After 990 a second castle, the Bouffay, stands at the corner by the water, and its men look at this one.
sites.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 26 (Fulcher's walled refuge), c. 28 (it falls, 919), c. 30 (Alan's earthwork and tower, about 940), c. 44 (the Bouffay, 990; of wood at first, it seems: fr.wikipedia Chateau du Bouffay)

sites.name: The moneyer's house
sites.see: A stone room near the count's house with a barred window: a charcoal hearth, a block with an iron die set in it, a man striking and a man feeding blanks, a third weighing what comes out. The new pennies say NAMNETVM round a cross. Old coin and foreign silver go into the pot at the rate chalked on the door.
sites.source: Pennies of Louis the Pious reading NAMNETVM (1.78 g) and of Charles the Bald reading NAMNETIS CIVITAS (1.62 g): Prou 1896, pp. 92-93. No mint under King Charles the Great, so nothing before 814. The closing year is ours: Charles the Bald died in 877 and nothing later was found by the dossier (?)

sites.name: Indre, the island monastery
sites.see: Three leagues below the city, a low green island in the stream with a church, a ring of wooden houses and fish weirs staked out into the current. Monks in the shallows hauling a net, herons, a bell over the water. In the guest house a foreign monk sits among stacked calfskins, writing with his sleeves tied back. It smells of river and smoked fish.
sites.source: Hermeland's monastery of about 673, three leagues below the city in fish-rich water, burned on 29 June 843 and never rebuilt: Chronicon Namnetense c. 6; fr.wikipedia Hermeland d'Indre. That a monk of Tours lodged there is ours

sites.name: Saints Donatian and Rogatian, outside the wall
sites.see: A basilica among graves on the road east of the city, where the two brothers of Nantes who died for the faith are buried. Stone coffins lie half out of the ground, older ones under them; a chapel of Saint Stephen stands to one side. Nearer the wall is Saint Cyr's little church with its own yard. The city buries its dead here, outside, as the Romans did. Yew, turned earth, a wind off the river.
sites.source: fr.wikipedia Basilique Saint-Donatien-et-Saint-Rogatien (four successive churches, Merovingian stone coffins, a pagan cemetery beneath; Saint Stephen's chapel); burial outside the walls at St Donatian's, St Cyr's and St Andrew's: Chronicon Namnetense c. 23; Miracula c. 3

sites.name: The Reze crossing
sites.see: A broad flat boat on a sloping hard at the downstream end of the strand, and the river beyond it split into channels by willow islands. The ferryman poles from sandbank to sandbank and rows the deep parts; a cart and two oxen stand aboard looking unhappy. On the far side the old south-bank port, a few roofs among Roman ruin, and the road to the salt country and Herio.
sites.source: Reze (Ratiatum), the old port on the south bank: fr.wikipedia Reze, Port de Nantes. No bridge is known in 793 (one is claimed under Alan the Great, a timber footway swept off by floods and ice (?): fr.wikipedia Pont de Pirmil). The ferry is ours; a Loire ferryman who wants his fare is in Ermentarius (dossier herio 3)

sites.name: The boat strand on the Erdre
sites.see: Where the little river comes in under the north-west tower: a muddy bank out of the tide's pull, with a barge on blocks, a boat upside down being tarred, and oak from up the Erdre stacked to season. Two men with adzes, a boy boiling pitch, shavings everywhere. The wall rises straight behind it.
sites.source: ours: no shipwright of Nantes is named (dossier 8). The workshops of the city paid toll (Chronicon Namnetense c. 14); the wall ran along the Erdre (fr.wikipedia Enceinte gallo-romaine de Nantes)

people.name: Odilard
people.trait: An old bishop in a church far grander than his city, who has outlasted three counts and expects to outlast the fourth; curious about any place a ship has been.
people.want: News from the sea, lamp oil and wax for Felix's church, and the old rights of his see (the toll, the fairs) back from the count.
people.fear: That the city is too big for its people: a wall nobody can man, and islands downriver full of monks nobody could help.
people.voice: Dry and unhurried, as if reading from a list; ends on the thing he actually wanted to ask.
people.looks: Past seventy, thin, a white tonsure, a plain wool tunic under a worn silk stole, a short staff with a horn crook, lamp-black on his cuffs.
knows: who is count this year and how long he is likely to last
what the church once held: tolls and fairs, the islands' fishing
which feasts fill the city, and when the pilgrims come
the bishops of the province of Tours, and who carries letters between them

ties.note: the toll was the church's once; the bishop reminds the toll man of it every quarter day
lets the foreign monk read in the cathedral's book chest, and asks him what Tours is saying
Tours is his metropolitan's city; from 796 the abbot of Saint Martin's is the loudest voice in the province
the cellarer of the salt island, in the next diocese south, sends him salt at Michaelmas and a list of what the island lacks (?)
her ale is on his table at feasts; he knows she hears what his clerks say there, and has them say it carefully

lines.greet: A Frisian, this far west. Then you have passed more of the king's toll benches than I have relics. Sit. What does the sea say?
lines.greet_again: You came back. Most shipmen see our sandbanks once and remember an errand somewhere else.
rumour: They say heathen ships burned a holy island in the English north. We have islands too, with monks on them, and it is the same sea.
The Bretons pay the king's tribute when a count is watching. No count can watch every year.
lines.stone: The red stone on the column came from Alexandria. They say it lights the nave by night. I still buy lamp oil, so judge for yourself.
lines.saying: Bishop Felix cut a channel and brought the river to the city. Since then every bishop of Nantes is expected to move water.
lines.farewell: Go with the ebb, and with God. Come at Saint John and you will see the city as full as it believes it is.

people.source: Real: bishop about 776 to about 800 (fr.wikipedia Liste des eveques de Nantes). Nothing but his name and years is known; his birth year is not, and the character is ours. The church's old claim to tolls and fairs: Chronicon Namnetense c. 14. The carbuncle: c. 1

people.name: Wido
people.trait: The king's count of the Breton march: a soldier who would rather count spears than pennies, pious in the way of a man who has been told his sins by an expert.
people.want: The march quiet, the king content, and somebody honest to tell him what the Breton shipmen are saying on the salt coast.
people.fear: That the Bretons gave up their weapons and kept their minds; that the heathen will come up his river while he is looking west.
people.voice: Short, even, a Frank's pride worn lightly; speaks of the king as of weather.
people.looks: About forty-five, broad, a clipped brown beard going grey, a riding cloak pinned at the shoulder, a long Frankish sword and a small book in a leather bag at his belt.
knows: the state of the march: which Breton chiefs have sworn and which only bowed
what the king has ordered for the river mouths and the coast watch
who may carry weapons out of the realm, and what it costs to be caught
what the toll brings in, to the sack

ties.note: the abbot of Tours wrote him a short book on the virtues and vices; Wido carries it and has read it more than once
the toll man serves him; the count is his lord and reads his tallies
the monk brought the abbot's book down the river and read it aloud to him the first time
the pilot told him which Breton masters could be asked for ships in 799; it was never paid for
from 814 the old emperor's cousin sits in exile on the salt island; the count of the march answers for what comes and goes on this coast, his letters with it (?)
the old count of Paris: they meet at the king's assemblies and agree about bishops (invented)
the count on the Garonne: Wido is praised for a cart of spears, and Seguin is written to about his manners

lines.greet: You are the merchant with the small boat. My toll man speaks of you. He speaks of everyone, but of you without spitting.
lines.greet_again: Back again. Good. A man who returns to a march town is either honest or owed money, and I can use both.
rumour: I rode the whole of Brittany. Every chief gave up his weapon with his name cut on it. Names are easy to cut.
Since the heathen came to the islands the king wants ships at every river mouth. He has not said who is to row them.
lines.book: Abbot Alcuin wrote me a book, so a man of war might know his sins by name. It is short. He knows how much a count reads.
lines.saying: A march is a door. Somebody must stand in it, and those behind him complain of the draught.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you speak with Breton masters on the salt coast, remember what they said and who said it. I pay for memory.

people.source: Real: Wido (Guy), who 'presided in the march of Brittany' in 799 (Annales regni Francorum 799), dead by 818 (fr.wikipedia Guy de Nantes). Who held Nantes before 799 is not known, so he is not met before that year. Alcuin's book for him: en.wikipedia Alcuin. His birth year is unknown; the character is ours

people.name: Eadhelm
people.trait: A Northumbrian monk of Saint Martin's at Tours, sent down the river to buy calfskins and find ships: exact about books, hopeless about boats, homesick for York's library.
people.want: Skins up the river before the scribes sit idle, finished books safely out to the bishops who asked for them, and a letter from York now and then.
people.fear: A book going into the sea; and that everything he remembers of York is already burned or changed.
people.voice: Quick and precise, counts things aloud, turns to complaint and then is ashamed of it; warms when asked what a book is.
people.looks: About thirty in 796, lean, fair hair round a tonsure, a dark patched habit with the sleeves tied back, ink to the second knuckle, a wax tablet on a cord and a wrapped book he does not put down.
knows: what a book is worth and to whom: the skins, the scribe's year, the cover
which bishop in the north has asked Tours for what, and who has paid
the price of calfskin at Nantes and of parchment at Tours
the abbeys' toll-free boats on the Loire and when the next one goes up
the news of York and Northumbria as far as letters bring it

ties.note: his abbot and his old master at York; he was one of the boys who followed him to Gaul
they were at the minster school at York together, and still write when a ship allows
the archbishop of York has a book promised from Tours, and Eadhelm is to find it a ship
the old bishop lets him read in the cathedral chest
read the abbot's little book to the count, and explained the hard words without seeming to
she feeds the carters who bring his skins and has not yet been paid for last autumn
a fellow Northumbrian who reads; they know the same psalter by its mistakes
the ferryman takes him and his skins to Indre and tells him, every time, to sit down
wrote to the widow at Bordeaux, in his best Latin, about the old poet's book; she answered in better (?)
the cooper makes his book boxes of waxed oak; Eadhelm measures each one and finds it a finger short

lines.greet: You have the look of a man with a dry hold. Good. I have four hundred calfskins and a river that runs the wrong way.
lines.greet_again: The small boat. Thank God. The last skipper stowed a psalter under his salt and told me it would keep the better.
rumour: The abbot has more letters than messengers. A ship that carries one north carries his thanks, and bishops honour those.
The master wants all scripture in one book, in letters a tired priest can read. It takes a herd of calves and two winters.
lines.york: At York the books had a room of their own. Here I keep them from the damp with my cloak. The cloak is losing.
lines.saying: Three fingers hold the pen and the whole body works. Tell that to the next man who calls writing light labour.
lines.worth: A boat is oak and a winter. This is a herd and a scribe's year. If one must go over the side, I know which the abbot would choose.
lines.farewell: If you come to York, look at the minster for me. Do not tell me what has changed.

people.source: invented, to place the spine's hook for the thread book_road (a monk who wants passage up the Loire with skins, or down with a finished book for a bishop in the north). Alcuin was abbot of Saint Martin's from 796 and brought English pupils to Tours (?). The scribe's complaint is a common colophon of the age, in our rendering (?)

people.name: Nanthard
people.trait: The count's toll-gatherer at the port: a Frank among Romans, proud of the king, exact to the halfpenny, with a memory for hulls and how deep they sit.
people.want: A tally nobody can fault, and to be remembered by the count for it.
people.fear: The bishop getting the toll back; a king's envoy opening his chest and finding it one penny light.
people.voice: Says the rule first and the kindness after, as if the kindness were also a rule.
people.looks: Mid-forties in 793, square, fair moustache in the Frankish fashion and a shaved chin, a good blue cloak, a tally stick as long as his forearm and a ring of keys.
knows: the toll on every good, and which charters free whom
every ship in the port, her master, and what she carried last time
when the salt and the wine are due and which abbey's boats pay nothing
what the count is asking about this month

ties.note: the count's man, and carries him the port's talk with the tally
the bishop says the toll was Saint Peter's; Nanthard says the chest is the king's
has drunk at her house every evening for ten years and never once been let off the reckoning
the ferryman lands people on the islands where no toll bench stands, and they both know it
the abbot who oversees the king's tolls in the northern ports is the name every toll man quotes (?)

lines.greet: The king's tenth, by ship or any other way. Since you came by ship we need not discuss the other ways.
lines.greet_again: The small boat again. You sit deeper than at Easter. I notice such things. It is all I am paid for.
rumour: Salt comes up from the bay after the Assumption. Buy before the abbey boats come. They pay no toll and so are never in a hurry.
The Bretons bring grain and take only salt. A man who wants one thing is hard to cheat. I respect it.
lines.pilgrims: At Saint John every trader in Gaul is a pilgrim. I count the bundles on the pilgrim's mule and believe accordingly.
lines.saying: A Frisian wears a short cloak so he can run from the toll. It has never once worked.
lines.farewell: Go on. The tide does not wait, and neither does the next ship's tenth.

people.source: invented: the office from Chronicon Namnetense c. 14 (the toll and the men who gather it). The tenth is the game's toll (npc_text_encounters.md 1.1). The short cloak is the Franks' old joke on Frisians, in the manner of Notker I.34 (Grant 1907); traders passing as pilgrims is King Charles's own complaint to Offa in 796

people.name: Paternus
people.trait: Ferryman at the Reze crossing and pilot of the river down to Batz: a Breton mother, a Nantes father, both tongues, and no opinion he will give away free.
people.want: His fare, from everyone; and a son-in-law who can read the water, since his daughters can and may not be paid for it.
people.fear: The river moving a bank in the night; being asked by the count to say which Breton said what.
people.voice: Slow, sideways, answers with a mark or a tide; laughs before the joke, not after.
people.looks: Around forty in 793, short and thick-armed, black hair cropped, bare legs burnt brown, a hooded cape of oiled wool and a long ash pole worn pale where his hands go.
knows: the channels among the islands this season, and the hour the flood reaches the city
the marks down the estuary: Indre, the long sands, Batz at the mouth
the Breton salt masters of Batz and Guerande by name, and what they will take for salt at the pan
who crossed to Reze this week and what they carried

ties.note: his dead wife's sister; he brings her the salt men and she brings him their debts
the toll man suspects the ferry of landing goods on the islands; he is right about one time in three
found the count Breton ships in 799 and was thanked in words
takes the monk and his skins to Indre, and has stopped trying to teach him to sit still in a boat
the bay pilot of the salt island: the river men say the bay men cannot read a river, and hear the same said of themselves at sea (?)
ferries the island's salt monk over on his way to Tours and back, and is set a riddle each time in place of half the fare (?)
the Garonne pilot calls the Loire a ditch with a tide in it; Paternus says the same of the Garonne, and adds the mud

lines.greet: You came up on the flood and touched nothing. Luck. The river keeps a dozen islands here and moves the small ones when nobody looks.
lines.greet_again: You again, and still afloat. Then you listened last time. Most pay me and then steer by their own opinion.
rumour: Batz is the mark at the mouth. Keep it north of you and wait for the flood. The ebb here has drowned better boats.
Indre lies three leagues down in the best fishing water on the river. The monks eat very well on fast days.
lines.fare: Counts and saints pay the ferry like anyone. I carried a relic over once and its keepers argued the fare. The relic said nothing.
lines.saying: The Loire is wide so that it can be shallow everywhere at once.
lines.bretons: My mother's people sell salt and keep quiet. If a Breton master tells you his price twice, the second is the true one.
lines.farewell: Go down on the first of the ebb, not the last. And if the water turns the colour of ale, you are over sand.

people.source: invented: nothing is written of pilots, bars or depths on the Loire (dossier 8). The estuary, the islands and the hard ascent: en.wikipedia Nantes; fr.wikipedia Estuaire de la Loire. Batz and Indre as marks: Chronicon Namnetense c. 5-6. A Loire ferryman who wanted his fare from a saint's servants is in Ermentarius (dossier herio 3). Unlock: unlock_pilot_loire in unlocks_793.json

people.name: Electa
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house by the carters' gate and the salt shed behind it: a widow with a head for reckonings, who remembers every face, what it drank and what it owes.
people.want: Her tallies paid by Michaelmas, the salt shed full before the abbey boats come, and a reason to think well of somebody.
people.fear: A bad year on the pans, when every salt man on her beam of chalk strokes goes home to the bay and does not come back.
people.voice: Brisk, teasing, never asks a question she does not already know half the answer to.
people.looks: Near forty in 793, strong and quick, dark hair under a linen cloth, a russet gown kilted for work, a chalk on a string round her neck and a ladle in her fist.
knows: the price of salt at the pan and at the gate, this week and last
who owes whom in the port, and who is about to sell cheap because of it
which carter came from Tours or Angers and what he saw on the road
where a paid-off shipman is sleeping, and whether he is worth hiring
what the player's own crew said after the third cup

ties.note: her dead sister's husband; they quarrel like family and trade like partners
he comes every evening; she lets him, and charges him full measure
feeds his carters on credit because he blushes when he asks
sends ale to the bishop's table on feast days, and hears what the clerks said at it
the monks' cellarer sells salt that paid no toll; she sells salt that did, and resents the difference (?)
a big Frisian house once bought her whole shed in August and paid at Easter; she has not forgotten either date (?)
he tubs her salt shed on a tally she chalks and he disputes

lines.greet: A stranger, and sober. Sit by the cask. The first cup is a halfpenny and the news comes with the second.
lines.greet_again: There you are. I kept your bench from a carter twice your size. You owe me a story from the north.
rumour: The salt men from the bay drink on credit until Michaelmas. If one offers you a pan cheap in August, ask what he owes me.
A measure of wine for a penny at the gate, and an honest one. Upriver they water it. Here the river does that for nothing.
lines.kept: Your man left his knife here at midsummer. I kept it. Tell him the next thing he leaves, I sell.
lines.saying: A carter tells you what the road cost him. A shipman tells you what the sea nearly did. Neither tells the price he got.
lines.friend: Sell your salt at Tours or sell it to me. I pay less. But I pay today, and I remember who dealt straight.
lines.farewell: Mind the sands. And come back before the chalk on your stroke wears off my beam.

people.source: invented: the ale-house keepers of the city are in Chronicon Namnetense c. 14. The measure of wine for a penny is Ermentarius on the market at Deas about 838 (dossier herio 4), carried back. Her house keeps the salt shed after her; from 836 its keeper holds Aldhelm's riddle of the wine cask (riddles_793.json)

people.name: Gunhard
people.trait: The bishop of a city caught between two counts and one open river: gentle, tired, and steadier than the men with swords.
people.want: Masons for the wall, peace between the counts, and the Saint John's gathering kept as it always was.
people.fear: Sails on a west wind on a feast day, with every door of the city open for pilgrims.
people.voice: Quiet, asks before he tells, and listens to the answer with his whole face.
people.looks: About fifty, slight, grey tonsure, a white linen alb and a faded green chasuble, a plain silver cross, hands that are never quite still.
knows: which count holds the city and which wants it, and where the Bretons stand
what has happened on the Rhine and the Seine, from the letters bishops send each other
the state of the wall, stone by stone, and the old entrance stopped with rubble
the feasts, and how many strangers each brings through the gates

ties.note: the abbot who took Saint Philibert off the island in 836; Gunhard defended him when people called it faint heart
the monk who is writing the saint's journey down has asked him what he saw of it
knows the missionary to the Danes only by letters passed between bishops, and prays for him by name (?)
the salt man who stayed on the island when the monks left; he brings the bishop the bay's news, and in 843 hides one of his clerks
a clerk of Rouen who saw his own city burn in 841 and carries the bishops' letters about it (?)
the count who holds the city for King Charles from 841; the bishop prays for him by name and begs him to make peace with Lambert

lines.greet: You come from the Rhine mouth? Then you have seen what I only read in letters. How long did Dorestat have, between the sail and the fire?
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Come in out of the street. You are the one visitor this week who wants nothing from the church but its news.
rumour: Two counts want this city and the king has chosen one. The other has friends among the Bretons. I say Mass for both and sleep badly.
The monks of Herio carried their saint inland seven years ago. People called it a faint heart. Nobody says so this summer.
lines.wall: There is an old doorway in the wall, stopped with rubble since my grandfather's day. I ask the count for masons. He asks me for prayers.
lines.saying: Lift up your hearts. We say it at every Mass, and each year it weighs a little more.
lines.farewell: Come for Saint John. The whole country comes. Whatever else is true of us, on that day the city is alive.

people.source: Real: Gunhard (Gohard), bishop 835 to 843, killed in his cathedral on Saint John's day 843 as he said 'Sursum corda', at Saint Ferreolus's altar in the left aisle (Chronicon Namnetense c. 5-6; Merlet 1896; fr.wikipedia Gohard de Nantes). The entrance long since blocked: c. 6. His birth year is unknown and the character is ours. He is a saint only from 1096

people.name: Alan Twisted-beard
people.trait: A Breton lord raised in exile at the English king's court, who took his city back with a sword and now needs it full of traders: blunt, practical, short of patience and silver.
people.want: Ships in the port, a roof on the cathedral, canons to sing in it, and a toll worth splitting.
people.fear: That he has won a ruin; that the Northmen were only the first to notice how much the river is worth.
people.voice: Says a thing once and plainly, in a Frankish learned among Englishmen; jokes at his own expense and nobody else's.
people.looks: About forty, big, a thick fair beard that grows crooked, a mail shirt under a plain red cloak, an English brooch, a sword worn at the hip and notched.
knows: who has come back to the city and who is still hiding upriver
what the toll is and how it is shared: a third his, a third the bishop's, a third the viscounts'
the English ports and the king's court there, from his years in exile
where the Northmen of the Loire went, and which of them stayed to trade

ties.note: Rollo's son William, the Northmen's count at Rouen, holds the Bretons' eastern edge by the king's gift of 933 and would like more of it (?)

lines.greet: A merchant. Good. I have a city with brambles in the church and no market. The toll is light this year, there being nothing to toll.
lines.greet_again: You came back, and with a cargo. Sit down. You are the second man this month to bring me something besides a complaint.
rumour: I grew up at the English king's court. There they build the wall first and the church inside it. I mean to do the same.
The Northmen held this river near twenty years and kept a market on it. Even wolves want salt.
lines.thorns: I cut my way to the cathedral door with a sword. It is the only fight I ever had where the other side could not hit back.
lines.saying: A third of the toll for me, a third for the bishop, a third for the viscounts. That way three men watch the toll man.
lines.farewell: Tell them in the north that Nantes has a lord and a market again. Say the lord first. It makes the second easier to believe.

people.source: Real: Alan Barbetorte, lord of Nantes and duke of the Bretons 937 to 952 (Chronicon Namnetense c. 27-36; fr.wikipedia Liste des comtes de Nantes). His return from King Athelstan's court: ages_793.json (Flodoard 936); that the king was his godfather is the chronicle's (?). The toll in three: c. 31. His birth year is not known. He is a Breton: 'romance' stands in because the roles table has no Breton people

people.name: Maurus
people.trait: The cooper by the port: makes salt tubs, wine casks and, for the monks, oak boxes that shut like a clam; staves them thin and swears thin is right.
people.want: Chestnut hoops from upriver before the vintage; a buyer from the Seine to say aloud that a Loire cask travels.
people.fear: A cask of his opening at sea under another man's cargo.
people.voice: Loud Romance over the noise of his own mallet; ends each sentence with a tap.
people.looks: About thirty-five, long-armed, a shaved head burnt brown, a leather apron black with pitch, a curved drawknife in his belt and a hoop over one shoulder.
knows: what a cask and a salt tub cost here, and how much each really holds
which shipmen ask for thick staves and what that says about their stowing
how to box a book against damp: oak, wax in the joints, never pine
who is loading for the Seine this month

ties.note: The Rouen cooper says Loire casks are staved too thin. Maurus says the Seine men build a cask like a church door and charge for the oak (?).
Her salt shed is tubbed by him, on a tally she chalks and he disputes.
Makes the monk's book boxes, and has been told four times that the last one was a finger too short.

lines.greet: Frisian? Then you have Seine casks aboard, thick as a wall. Knock on one of mine. Hear that? That is a cask. The other is a tree.
lines.greet_again: Did they hold? They held. Tell that to the cooper at Rotomagus, slowly, in front of people.
rumour: The English monk wants a box for a book again. Oak, waxed, a finger longer than the last. For one book. I have housed families in less.
Salt tubs are short this year. Whoever brings me hoop wood before the Assumption names his price in tubs.
lines.saying: Thin stave, tight hoop, dry wine.
lines.farewell: Stow them bung up. And if a man on the Seine asks who made them, say it twice.

people.source: invented (Maurus, a Romance name of the time: names_placeholder.json), to give the Rotomagus cooper's tie its man. Casks, tubs and hoops: Design/economy_and_trade.md; no craftsman of Nantes is named in these years. The quarrel over staves is the game's (?).

people.name: Rainald
people.trait: Count of Herbauge, the shore south of the Loire, and from 841 King Charles's count at Nantes: a fighter who rides to where the ships are, with enemies on three sides.
people.want: Lambert kept out of the city; the Bretons kept west of the Vilaine; one summer without sails.
people.fear: Being caught between the Bretons and a river, which is how it ends.
people.voice: Hoarse and quick, a horseman's Frankish; counts men, not pennies.
people.looks: About forty, lean, a cropped dark beard, mail under a mud-splashed green cloak, a horseman's long spurs and a spear he does not put down indoors.
knows: where the Northmen landed on the salt island in 835 and how they were beaten
who holds for King Charles on the Loire and who for Lambert
the fords of the Vilaine and who watches them
how many armed men the abbey of the island kept

ties.note: Fought for the abbot's island on the saint's feast in 835, and told him afterwards to take the saint ashore.
The bishop prays for him by name and asks him, each time, to make peace with Lambert.

lines.greet: Shipman. What sails did you see between the island and the river mouth? Count them for me again, and slowly.
lines.greet_again: You counted true last time. That is worth a cup. What is in the bay this week?
rumour: On the saint's feast nine ships came to the island and we beat them on the sand. The abbot counted the dead. I counted how near it was.
Lambert wants this city and will take help from anyone to get it. Anyone. Remember I said so.
lines.saying: A count on a horse can be in one place. A fleet can be in any.
lines.farewell: If you pass the island, tell the salters I have not forgotten them. Then tell them not to count on it.

people.source: Rainald (Renaud), count of Herbauge: fought the Northmen on Herio in 835 (Annals of Angouleme; Ermentarius, Miracula II, preface); count of Nantes from 841; killed in May 843 fighting Lambert and the Bretons, at Messac or near Blain (Chronicon Namnetense c. 4-5; Annales Bertiniani 843). The Namnetis story 'Saint John's day' has his death; the Herio file names him as namnetis.rainald. Dates from memory, to be checked (?). His birth year, looks and words are invented.

stories.title: A herd and a scribe's year
stories.summary: From 796 the monks of Saint Martin's at Tours, under Abbot Alcuin, write books for half the bishops of the north, and all of it passes Nantes: calfskins going up the Loire, finished books coming down. Eadhelm, an English monk with no sea legs, needs a small dry boat and a skipper who understands that the thing in the wrapped box is worth more than the hull.
stories.picture: The guest house on Indre in grey river light: stacked calfskins to the rafters, a thin monk with ink on his hands holding out a wrapped book to a shipman, and through the open door a small boat at the island's stage with her hold open.

beats.text: Eadhelm has four hundred calfskins bought from the Breton cattle country and the abbey's own boat is not due for a month. He asks for passage up the river to the landing below Tours, eleven days against the stream with men hauling, or for the skins to be sold him at a fair price if you have any aboard. He pays in the abbot's thanks and a little silver. (The spine's flag bk_parchment is set when skins or parchment are carried for a church.)

A small book comes down from Tours for Count Wido: Abbot Alcuin's on the virtues and the vices, written short for a man of war. Eadhelm is to read it to him and is afraid to go alone. If you stand by, you hear what a book is worth to a man who cannot write one, and the count learns your face. (Sets bk_knows_worth.)

A finished book for a bishop in the north lies wrapped in waxed linen in a box of oak: a gospel book for the archbishop at York while Eadhelm lives, later a whole Bible in one volume in the clear Tours hand. No abbey boat goes to sea. He asks you to carry it, and tells you three times not to stow it under the salt.
At the toll house on the Canche a book is a thing the king's men do not know how to price. A letter from Tours passes it free; without one, the toll man guesses, and guesses high.
The archbishop's clerks at York unwrap the box in the minster porch. Sigewine reads the first leaf aloud and asks after Eadhelm by name, and whether he is still seasick on a river. (Sets bk_carried.)

Eadhelm hears how it went. If the book came safe he writes your name in the margin of the abbey's list of friends, in small letters, and shows you where. If it did not, he says nothing for a long time, and then asks what the sea was like that day.
The schoolmaster at Saint-Wandrille turns the leaves of a Tours book for a long time without reading a word. Then he asks who ruled the lines.
Eadhelm's letter about the old poet's book has reached the widow by the Broken Tower. She reads it to the room and corrects one case ending.
The salt brother sat two winters in the school at Tours. He sends salt up the Loire for the scribes' table and asks whether the Englishman still gets sick on a river.

endings.how: Took the skins up the river and the book north, and brought both in dry.
endings.text: Tours trusts the house with its books. Every second summer there is a box waiting on Indre and a bishop at the other end who receives a merchant as he would a guest.
endings.reward: A standing commission from Tours (a book to carry each second year, paid 60 to 120 d and in standing with the church of the port it goes to); Eadhelm a fast friend; a letter that passes books free at Frankish tolls; the text alcuin_793 read out and explained.

endings.how: Carried the book north and sold it to a richer buyer than the one it was written for.
endings.text: It fetches more than the boat. The letter that comes down the Loire the next spring is addressed to the bishop of Nantes and names the house. Eadhelm will not look up when you come in.
endings.reward: Silver, once: the price of a book and more (360 d and upward). No church in the province of Tours gives the house lodging or credit for a generation; the spine's flag bk_lost.

endings.how: The book went into the sea, or was spoiled by salt and water in the hold.
endings.text: Eadhelm asks what the sea was like that day and writes it down. The scribes begin again. If you offer the skins for the second copy, he takes them, and after a while he takes your hand too.
endings.reward: Nothing but the debt; the house may pay for the skins of the new copy (about 240 d) and be forgiven, with Eadhelm easy again and the book road open; the spine's flag bk_lost until then.

stories.reward: The book road's western end: a trade no rival understands, a monk at Indre who is glad to see you, and bishops from Tours to York who know the house's name.

stories.title: Names on the spears
stories.summary: In 799 Count Wido rides through all Brittany and comes home with the weapons of the chiefs who yielded, each marked with its owner's name, to lay before the king. On the salt coast the Breton masters who sell you salt want one thing more than silver: to know whose name was really in the cart. Paternus the ferryman has kin on both sides of the question.
stories.picture: The yard of the count's house on a wet autumn day: an ox cart heaped with spears, swords and round shields, a clerk reading scratched names off the shafts to a man with a wax tablet, and a ferryman watching from the gate with his pole on his shoulder.

beats.text: The cart stands in the yard for a week before it goes to the king. A clerk reads the names cut on each weapon and another writes them down. Anybody with business in the yard can hear the list, and you have business: the count wants to know what the Breton masters are saying where you buy salt.

Paternus asks, looking at the water, whether a certain name was read. It is his mother's brother's lord, a chief by the salt pans of Batz. If the name was in the cart the man has bowed, and his people may sell to Franks in peace. If it was not, somebody gave up another man's spear.
On the bay a Breton salt master offers salt at the pan's own price to a man who will tell him the list. He has already heard two lists and they do not agree. He says his price twice.

The count asks what you heard on the salt coast, and who said it. He is courteous, and he has a toll-free writ on the table that is not yet sealed. In 811 an army goes against the Bretons for breach of faith; what you told him, or did not, is part of why it goes where it goes.
On the Garonne Count Seguin has heard of the cart of named spears and of the king's praise. He asks what the Bretons really gave up, and seems to hope it was little.
Count Stephen saw the cart at the king's assembly. He says a spear with a name on it is a promise, and that he has a chest of promises at home.

endings.how: Told the Bretons the true list and told the count only what any man on the quay could have told him.
endings.text: The salt masters of Batz sell to the house first and at the pan's price, and send word down the coast that the Frisian is a man who repeats what he hears and nothing more. The count is civil and seals nothing.
endings.reward: act:buy_at_source for salt at Namnetis and on the bay at the cheap price in every season, inherited; Paternus a fast friend and a pilot who takes no fee; no charter from the count.

endings.how: Carried the count the names and words of the Breton masters, season after season.
endings.text: The writ is sealed: the house passes the toll bench at Nantes without opening a sack. On the bay the Bretons still sell, at the price they give strangers, and Paternus ferries you over without a word.
endings.reward: A toll-free charter for Namnetis while Wido lives (act:show_charter), renewed by his heirs for a gift; standing with the Franks of the Loire; Paternus and the salt masters cool for a generation.

endings.how: Told neither side anything, and bought salt at the gate like anybody else.
endings.text: Nothing happens to the house in 811. Electa remarks that it is the first time she has seen a shipman keep his mouth shut for three years together, and stands a cup.
endings.reward: Nothing lost: Electa friendly, one free rumour at each call; the choice stays open to the heir when the march next stirs.

stories.reward: The salt coast's trust or the count's seal, and with either a man at Nantes who will remember which you chose.

stories.title: Saint John's day
stories.summary: A merchant who has seen Dorestad burn knows what a fleet does to a rich town with its doors open. In the summer of 843 Nantes has two counts at each other's throats, an old doorway in the wall stopped with rubble, and the whole country coming in for the feast. Bishop Gunhard will hear a warning; whether the city can use one is another matter.
stories.picture: The cathedral's west door at dusk on a midsummer day, seen from the river gate: the tin roof still bright, smoke beginning behind it, long ships pulling off down the brown river with people sitting very still amidships, and one ladder left leaning on the wall.

beats.text: Gunhard asks what you saw on the Rhine: how long between the sail and the fire, what was saved and what was not. He writes nothing down. He takes you to see the stopped doorway in the wall and asks what masons cost where you come from. (If you tell him plainly, the spine's flag df_warned is set.)

Count Renaud is dead at Blain since the feast of Donatian and Rogatian, killed by Lambert and the Bretons. Nobody is count. The ale-house says Lambert means to have the city by any hand that will give it him. The salt men from the bay have not come up this year.

The eve of the feast. The streets are full, the gates stand open for pilgrims, and there is a west wind up the river. A ship lying at the port this night can be out on the dawn ebb with whoever she can carry, or stay and see the feast.

This year the Northmen came up to Nantes on Saint John's day with sail and oar, climbed the wall with ladders and broke in by the old doorway, and killed the bishop at his altar and the people in the church, and went off at dusk with a great many captives. Five days after they burned Indre.

The fleet lies at the salt island and falls out over the spoil like dogs at meat. At low water some captives walk off across the sands, one with the cathedral's great Bible hung on his neck. The rest are for holding or for selling, and a ship that comes with silver may buy them back, dear.

On the last day of September, the church's own dedication day, Bishop Susan of Vannes cleanses the cathedral of blood, and Mass is said again. Those who were bought back stand at the front. Somebody has set the Bible on the altar, salt-stained along one edge.
Einold has a letter for Bishop Gunhard and no boat for the Loire. It says what he saw in May of 841, in order, without one adjective.
The news of Nantes comes down the coast with the salt. The wine sellers ask how wide the Loire is at the city, and then look at their own river.
At the house by the Little Bridge they want the story of Saint John's day told twice. The second time nobody drinks.

endings.how: Warned the bishop in time and paid for masons to wall the old doorway (the work namnetis.work.doorway).
endings.text: The ladders still come over the wall, but not the rush through the breach. More people reach the river gate and the boats than would have. Gunhard dies at his altar all the same; he would not leave the Mass. Afterwards the city cuts the house's name on the new stones.
endings.reward: Standing with every Christian of the Loire, greatly and for the heir too; what the house had stored in the city is spared; a place in the cathedral's prayers by name; lodging and sanctuary at Nantes for good.

endings.how: Sailed to Herio with silver after the feast and bought captives back.
endings.text: You bring home as many as the boat will carry, and their kin pay what they can, which is less than you paid. In every street somebody knows whose child came back in the Frisian's boat.
endings.reward: The deed of ransoming, told across the region; half the silver back at once and the rest as debts honoured over years; a family in each quarter of the city that will store, lodge and stand surety for the house.

endings.how: Bought the spoil of Nantes cheap on the strand at Herio and sold it elsewhere.
endings.text: Altar silver and good cloth at a third of their worth, and the men selling do not haggle. In a port far enough off it is only plate. At Nantes it is known by its marks, and so are you.
endings.reward: A very good cargo (church_plate and cloth far under price); plate from a church marks its seller: shunned at Namnetis and cool across the province of Tours until the pieces are given back.

endings.how: Left on the ebb before the feast with whoever would come.
endings.text: Most would not: it was Saint John's day. The few who came are alive, and one of them is a clerk with the keys of the book chest in his sleeve, who never forgives himself and never forgets you.
endings.reward: A clerk of Nantes as the house's friend and reader (Latin read for nothing here); a passenger's fare in gratitude; no blame and no glory.

stories.reward: What a merchant who had seen Dorestad could do for Nantes: a wall, a ransom or only a boat, and a city that remembers which.

stories.title: The leaf in the salt shed
stories.summary: Aldhelm's riddle whose answer is salt sends its solver to where salt is made. Until 835 that is a monk of the pans on Herio; when the monks leave their island the leaf comes to Nantes, to the keeper of the salt shed behind the ale-house, who cannot read it and uses it to wedge a tally board.
stories.picture: The salt shed behind the ale-house: grey sacks to the roof, a tally board on the wall held level by a folded strip of parchment, and a woman with chalk on a string reaching up to pull the strip out.

beats.text: A monk on his abbey's business has Aldhelm's riddle of salt: once I was water, full of scaly fish. Whoever answers it is told the next leaf waits where salt is made.
A monk of the salt pans has the second leaf, the riddle of the wine cask, and gives it to whoever names the answer to the first.

The monks are gone from the island with their saint. The keeper of the salt shed had a strip of parchment from one of them, in payment of a reckoning; it is behind the tally board. A reader aboard, or a clerk for a cup, makes it out: Aldhelm's riddle of the cask. (The effect is give_text aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria, as unlocks_793.json has it.)
Where the casks are filled the third leaf waits, the riddle of the glass cup, and at Colonia the last, whose answer is pepper.
At the fair of Saint Denis the cask's answer is the second of four. The abbey's man does not care where you had the leaf, only that you can say it.

endings.how: Had the leaf read at Nantes, answered it, and followed it up the Rhine.
endings.text: The salt shed's keeper wants to know what the scratches said. Told that it is a cask speaking, she says she has known casks that would not shut up either, and asks for the strip back to wedge the board.
endings.reward: The text aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria in the chest and its riddle (pays a little silver when answered); the next step of the set salt_to_pepper, whose end is the reward rw_right_pepper.

endings.how: Could not read it, and bought the strip anyway for a halfpenny.
endings.text: It lies in the chest until somebody aboard has Latin. The keeper thinks you a fool and likes you the better for paying.
endings.reward: The text in the chest, unread until learned.latin or a reader aboard; the alewife's house one step friendlier.

stories.reward: The second leaf of the salt-to-pepper chain, and a reason to learn Latin or keep a monk aboard.

stories.title: Brambles in the nave
stories.summary: In 937 Alan comes home from England, beats the Northmen in Saint Aignan's meadow and finds a city nobody has lived in for years: no market, no toll, no roof on the cathedral. The first salt ship up the river after that can ask almost anything of a lord who needs traders more than he needs silver.
stories.picture: The cathedral's west front under a white sky, roofless, the doorway choked with bramble: a big bearded man in mail hacking at the thorns with a sword, a handful of armed men behind him, and far down the empty street a single mast showing over the broken wall.

beats.text: There is no toll bench, no porters and no roof to sell under. Poor Bretons from the fields come down to look at the ship. A man in mail with a crooked beard walks down from the cathedral and asks what you carry and what you would want to come again.

The nave is open to the sky and the brambles are head high. Alan tells how he was dying of thirst on the hill before the fight and prayed, and Saint Mary opened a spring; he says it flatly, as a man reports a fact he does not expect to be believed. He wants a roof, and canons to sing under it.

The earthwork is up and the tower stands. Four canons have come home: Letard the archdeacon, Oger, Hugh, and Durand whom they call Pabion. The toll is shared in three. Alan asks whether the house will take a plot inside the bank and bring its friends.

Alan is dead. Three sacks of pennies go up the river to Fulk of Anjou, the boy's guardian, who is playing at tables when they come and says no man in the kingdom is so rich as he who holds Nantes. The house's plot and its terms were Alan's word: they stand, if somebody speaks for them.
Rollo's son William holds Rotomagus and, by the king's gift, a piece of the Bretons' land. He asks what Alan has in his river: ships, walls, friends. He asks pleasantly.
The Loire is open again, and the island's salt goes north in Breton hulls for the first time in a lifetime. The salters ask who takes the toll at Nantes now, and how much.

endings.how: Came with the first cargoes, took a plot inside the earthwork and paid toward the cathedral roof.
endings.text: The house has a booth by the gate before there is a market to put it in, and its name in the canons' book. When the sacks of pennies go up to Anjou, the toll man still waves its ships through for a third less than anyone's.
endings.reward: A plot at Namnetis for nothing and the toll lightened by a third for the house and its heir; Alan a fast friend; standing with the church of Nantes; the work namnetis.work.roof counted as begun.

endings.how: Sold one cargo dear to a town that had nothing, and sailed.
endings.text: Salt and iron tools at a hungry town's price. Alan pays without a word and does not ask you to come again. The next ship in gets the plot.
endings.reward: One very good sale (double the market's price, once); no plot, no lightened toll; Alan cool.

endings.how: Had traded with the Northmen of the Loire in their years, and it is known.
endings.text: A Breton who tilled under Incon points you out on the strand. Alan hears it, looks at you a while, and says that even wolves want salt, and that you will pay the full toll like a wolf.
endings.reward: Trade allowed at full toll and no favours; the Norse-speaking masters who stayed on the river deal with the house as an old acquaintance (one more rumour, and their prices).

stories.reward: A place in a city at the moment it begins again: a plot, a light toll and a lord's friendship, or one hard bargain.

works.name: A share of the salt shed
works.what: Room of your own in the stone shed behind the ale-house, under Electa's key and her chalk: salt bought at the pan in autumn waits there dry until the slaughter months, when it is dear.
works.needs: Electa, or whoever keeps her house, at least easy with you.
works.gives: Store up to six units at Namnetis (act:store); salt kept here does not take the damp. Lost in the sack of 843 unless the doorway was walled.
works.picture: A dim stone shed with grey sacks stacked on a plank floor, a chalk mark on the nearest stack, and a woman turning a big key in the door.
works.source: works_793.json store_corner; the shed is ours

works.name: A salt pan on the bay
works.what: A set of clay beds with its hut on the shore by Batz, worked by a Breton pan man for a share: the sun and the wind do the rest. Such pans were bought, sold and given by charter.
works.needs: The leave of the lord of the shore and a pan man who will work it: the Breton masters at least easy with you (the story 'Names on the spears' ended straight makes it sure).
works.gives: Each autumn 16 sacks of bay salt wait at Namnetis in the house's name; unfetched salt is sold there at the cheap price. Lost for some years to raids on the bay.
works.picture: Flat grey shore cut into square shallow pools shining white at the edges, a man with a long wooden rake drawing salt into a heap, a turf hut and the sea far out.
works.source: works_793.json salt_pan; 54 salt-works at Guerande and Batz in the Redon charters, 9th-10th centuries (fr.wikipedia Marais salants de Guerande; dossier 4). Whether pans were worked there in 793 itself is not shown (?)

works.name: Masons for the old doorway
works.what: An entrance in the city wall, stopped long ago with loose rubble, taken down to its sill and built up again in mortared stone the full thickness of the wall. Bishop Gunhard has asked the counts for it and been given prayers.
works.needs: Gunhard friendly, and the work finished before midsummer 843.
works.gives: On Saint John's day 843 the wall is climbed but not breached: the house's stores in the city are spared and more of the people reach the boats (the ending 'the_doorway'). Standing with the bishop and the townsfolk rises at once.
works.picture: A stretch of high grey Roman wall with a patch of new pale stone in the shape of a door, two masons on a timber stage, and a bishop below looking up with his hand shading his eyes.
works.source: works_793.json wall_share. In 843 the raiders 'broke through an entrance long since blocked': Chronicon Namnetense c. 6. That it could have been walled in time is the game's own device

works.name: A great Bible for Saint Peter's
works.what: All of scripture in one volume, written at Tours in the clear new hand on the skins of a herd, bound in boards, for the cathedral's altar. The house pays for the skins and the scribes' keep; Eadhelm or his successors see it made.
works.needs: The story 'A herd and a scribe's year' ended with the book carried; the bishop at least friendly.
works.gives: Standing with the church of Nantes rises greatly and a little across the region; the bishop a friend; the house may read in the cathedral (a text for the chest) and an heir be schooled there. In 843 it is the book a captive carries home over the sands on his neck.
works.picture: A very large book lying open on a marble altar under hanging gold crowns, two columns of small even writing on each page, a clerk turning a leaf with both hands.
works.source: works_793.json book. The cathedral's great Bible, carried off in 843, brought back over the sands on a captive's neck and still kept about 1050: Chronicon Namnetense c. 7. Where it was made is not recorded: that it came from Tours, and from this house's gift, is the game's own (?)

works.name: A house for Saint John's pilgrims
works.what: A roofed hall with straw, a hearth and a keeper beside Saint John's church, for the strangers who come from far cities for the vigil and now sleep against the wall.
works.needs: A plot from the bishop: standing with the church of the port.
works.gives: Standing with the Christians of the port and its region rises much, and alms count each year it is kept; a sick man of the crew is healed there for nothing (act:heal); one more rumour at each call, and three at midsummer.
works.picture: A long low thatched hall by a small church at dusk on midsummer eve: pilgrims with staffs coming in at the door, a woman ladling from a pot, candles lit in the church porch behind.
works.source: works_793.json hospice. Pilgrims from far cities on Saint John's day and the night vigil: Chronicon Namnetense c. 6; Miracula c. 4. No hospice of Nantes is recorded in these years: ours

works.name: A roof for the burned cathedral
works.what: Oak for the trusses floated down the Erdre, and shingle, since nobody can pay for tin again: the nave of Saints Peter and Paul closed against the weather for the first time since the Northmen burned it.
works.needs: Alan or his heirs holding the city; the brambles cut.
works.gives: The cathedral site works again with its feast days; the house is buried there and names a canon; standing with the Christians of the port and the region rises greatly, and the bishop is a friend to the heir too.
works.picture: The roofless nave from inside, new pale rafters going up against the sky, carpenters astride the ridge, and on the floor below a heap of cut bramble burning.
works.source: works_793.json church_rebuilt. The cathedral burned in 919 and stood roofless in 937: Chronicon Namnetense c. 28, 30; its east end was rebuilt by Guerech, 981-988: c. 42. Shingle for tin is ours

ships.note: The river's fishing and ferrying boat: the fishermen of the islands and the monks of Indre use nothing else. Always one for sale on the strand after the shad run.
ships.picture: A small open boat drawn up on a sandbank with a net drying over her side and a willow island behind.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat; the river's fishermen: Merlet 1896 (dossier 3). No boat of Nantes has been found: the type stands in

ships.how: built to order over a winter | bought second-hand
ships.note: The Loire's own carrier: flat, towed up to Angers and Tours by men on the bank, drifting down with wine. The boat strand on the Erdre builds them from oak brought down that river.
ships.picture: A long flat barge with a short towing mast lying at the strand under the wall, casks in a row along her bottom and a coiled hauling line on her bow.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json river_barge. About 955 four barges of great fish went up to Fulk of Anjou from Nantes, in the French version of the chronicle (Chronicon Namnetense c. 37). The Loire barge of 793 is not described anywhere (?)

ships.note: The abbeys' boats, toll-free on the Loire by the king's grant, go up to Tours and beyond: passage and a little cargo can be had aboard one for a gift to the house that owns her.
ships.picture: A slim river ship under eight oars with an awning aft, a cross painted on her bow, passing the toll bench without slowing while the toll man watches.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json river_estate_ship. Saint Philibert's abbey had six boats toll-free on the Loire and its rivers, confirmed in 826 (dossier herio 4); that Saint Martin's had the like is from memory (?)

ships.note: The salt boat of the bay and the Breton coast: a mast and yard, a sail, an anchor, a steersman and a man in the bow. Breton masters sell an old one when the grain trade has been good.
ships.picture: A round-bowed sailing boat lying to an anchor off the strand, her yard lowered, grey salt sacks under hides amidships and a man in the bow with a sounding pole.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship. Breton ships with yards, sails and anchors, a steersman and a bow lookout, about 838-840: Ermentarius I.81 (dossier herio 3-4)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A sea-going hull can be laid down on the Erdre strand if the buyer brings his own pattern and pays for the oak in advance: the wrights here are river men and say so. Not in the years the city lies waste (853-867, 919-936).
ships.picture: The ribs of a deep beamy hull on blocks under the city wall, twice the height of the barge beside her, two wrights arguing over a plank with a stranger.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json north_sea_merchant_ship. No sea-going ship is recorded as built at Nantes: ours (?)

ships.note: In the Northmen's years on the Loire a ship of theirs can be bought on the strand from a crew that is breaking up, for silver by weight and no questions either way.
ships.picture: A long low clinker ship hauled half out on the strand below a roofless church, her mast down, shields off, two men stripping her of gear while a third weighs silver.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship. The Northmen held Nantes 919-937 (Chronicon Namnetense c. 28-29) and asked for a market on a Loire island in 873 (Annales Bertiniani 873). The sale of a ship is ours

sayings.text: The world has night; the hall keeps the day.
sayings.source: Venantius Fortunatus on Bishop Felix's church, quoted by Merlet 1896; the dossier's own rendering

sayings.text: No man in the kingdom is so rich as he who holds Nantes.
sayings.source: Said by Fulk of Anjou when three sacks of the city's pennies were brought to him at his game of tables, about 955: Chronicon Namnetense c. 37, our rendering

sayings.text: They fought over it like dogs at meat.
sayings.source: Of the raiders dividing the spoil of Nantes on the island: Chronicon Namnetense c. 7, our rendering

sayings.text: What is a ship? A wandering house, a lodging anywhere, a traveller who leaves no footprint.
sayings.source: Alcuin, Disputatio Pippini cum Albino (about 790), our rendering from memory (?); said here by the monk of Tours

sayings.text: Three fingers hold the pen and the whole body works.
sayings.source: A scribe's complaint written at the end of many books of the 8th and 9th centuries, our rendering (?)

sayings.text: A Frisian wears a short cloak so he can run from the toll.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the Franks' mockery of the Frisians' short cloaks is Notker I.34 (Grant 1907)

sayings.text: The Loire is wide so that it can be shallow everywhere at once.
An unlettered king is a crowned ass.
sayings.source: Laid to Fulk the Good of Anjou, guardian of Nantes 952-960, by the Deeds of the Counts of Anjou, written in the 12th century: LATER, our rendering from memory (?). Heard at Nantes only from 952

sayings.text: Tell the count the great stake at the river's mouth has fallen.
sayings.source: What Fulk's wife told him in 960, knowing his sloth, to make him move against the Northmen: the stake fixed in the Loire's mouth was said to scare them. Chronicon Namnetense c. 38, our rendering. A byword at Nantes for the one message that gets a lord out of his chair

easter_eggs.text: On a marble column in the cathedral sits a red stone from Alexandria that is said to light the church by night. The clerks still fill the lamps.
easter_eggs.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 1 (the carbuncle); the lamps are ours

easter_eggs.text: An old man on the strand tells how a ship with Irish wares once took a holy abbot aboard here by the bishop's and the count's order, and the sea threw her back on the sand and would not float her until he was set ashore.
easter_eggs.source: Jonas, Life of St Columban c. 47, tr. Munro (about 610). The ship driven back is from the same chapter, from memory (?)

easter_eggs.text: A man walking through Saint Cyr's graveyard by the wall says a blessing for the dead as he goes, and hears them answer: amen, amen.

About the year 1000, on Saint John's night, a knight of the count's household and a woman are found stuck fast together like dogs, and stay so until the next sunset, when the clerks of the church beat them both. The ale-house does not tire of it for a generation.
easter_eggs.source: Miracula ecclesiae Namnetensis c. 4 (the knight is named Nominoe, of Count Judicael's household). Shown from 992

easter_eggs.text: Built into the river wall, upside down, is a cut stone that names the god Vulcan and the people of the port. The porters touch it for luck and call it the smith.
easter_eggs.source: Roman dedications to Vulcan, Mars Mullo and Minerva are known from Nantes (fr.wikipedia Histoire de Nantes); one names the people of the port, from memory (?). That it sat in the wall, and the porters' habit, are ours

easter_eggs.text: After 952, outside the walls by night, a host of riders is heard passing and nothing is seen. It stops when Alan's body is moved from Saint Donatian's, where it would not stay buried, to Notre-Dame.

At Angers they show two plates of lead that lay with a bishop's bones: one says 'the humble Gunhard', the other 'father and martyr'. People there say he took up his head, walked to the Loire, and a boat with no crew brought him upriver.
easter_eggs.source: Merlet 1896 (the lead plates); fr.wikipedia Gohard de Nantes (the legend, LATER). Shown from 844

easter_eggs.text: On the hill above Saint Aignan's meadow a spring runs that the townsfolk call Saint Mary's. They say it opened when Alan, thirsty before the fight, prayed for water.
One of the four canons who came home about 940 is Durand, whom everyone calls Pabion. Nobody will say why, least of all Durand.
easter_eggs.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 31 (the names: Letard the archdeacon, Oger, Hugh, Durand called Pabion); the silence is ours

unlocks.what: The Loire mouth and the bay of the salt, by heart
unlocks.how: Hire Paternus (or the pilot after him) on three calls and come through without touching, or sail the estuary three times end to end.
unlocks.gives: unlock_pilot_loire in unlocks_793.json: no pilot's fee on this water, the bar passed as 'sure', the tide window shown before the course is set; inherited.

unlocks.what: The Breton salt masters' own price
unlocks.how: End 'Names on the spears' straight: tell the Bretons the true list and the count nothing he could not hear on the quay.
unlocks.gives: act:buy_at_source for sea_salt at Namnetis at the cheap price in every season; hire_pilot here costs nothing; inherited.

unlocks.what: A toll-free writ for Namnetis under the count's seal
unlocks.how: End 'Names on the spears' as the count's ear; renewed by each new count for a gift.
unlocks.gives: act:show_charter at namnetis.toll: toll 0 here while a Frankish count holds the city (to 850).

unlocks.what: A letter from Saint Martin's that passes books free
unlocks.how: End 'A herd and a scribe's year' with the book carried.
unlocks.gives: Books and parchment in the hold pay no toll in Frankish ports; a commission from Tours each second year; flag bk_carried.

unlocks.what: Aldhelm's riddle of the wine cask
unlocks.how: From 836, ask at the ale-house about the strip behind the tally board, with the salt riddle answered.
unlocks.gives: give_text aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria (text.aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria in unlocks_793.json); the next step of the set salt_to_pepper.

unlocks.what: The house's name cut in the city wall and said in the cathedral's prayers
unlocks.how: Pay for the work namnetis.work.doorway before midsummer 843 and end 'Saint John's day' by it.
unlocks.gives: Lodging and sanctuary at Namnetis for good (act:lodge, act:sanctuary); standing with the Christians of the Loire inherited by the heir at full, not half.

unlocks.what: A plot inside Alan's earthwork and a third off the toll
unlocks.how: End 'Brambles in the nave' as first in.
unlocks.gives: A plot at Namnetis for nothing (works_793.json plot); toll here lightened by a third for the house; inherited once.
